title: Building Your Resume
hook: Ulric sees the kayak’s real resume in six muddy return cards clipped to a nail.
counterintuition: Most teams assume identity comes from positioning. But actually the market grants identity through repeated hires in similar circumstances.
tryThisNow: List three times someone chose the same product or service. Write the situation beside each one and circle the progress that repeats.
keyTakeaway: An offering’s resume is the pattern of jobs buyers repeatedly trust it to do, and that earned record should discipline promises, redesigns, and expansion.

breakdown.fastRead:
Ulric reads six muddy kayak return cards and notices the same note: safe first paddle with nervous guests. The rental shop thought its resume was fast boats and scenic water. The market had written a narrower one. A product's real identity is not what the team claims on a poster. It is what buyers keep hiring it to do when pressure repeats. One story can inspire. A pattern earns trust.

That is why the team should name the pattern before it writes the promise.
breakdown.deepRead:
A resume is an earned record. It says what a product or service has proven it can do in the situations buyers care about. Positioning can promise many things. The resume is narrower because it comes from repeated hires, not internal ambition.

At 4:40 p.m., Sonia wipes polish from her thumb in a shoe repair shop while a customer points to cracked boots. "You saved these before my last two inspections," he says. He is not buying leather work in general. He is hiring the shop to make him look squared away when his uniform gets judged. Three visits say more than any tagline.

Ulric's return cards also show what the team should ignore. One guest praised the color of the boats. Another liked the snack shelf. Those comments matter, but they do not yet form the resume. The repeated hire is the safer first paddle. The shop should protect that trust before chasing every compliment.

With the work in front of you, the move is to look for repetition with context attached. Who rehired, in what circumstance, after which pressure, and for what progress. If the same job appears across similar situations, the offering has earned that line on its resume. The limit is false unity. Repeated use does not prove one job if the circumstances differ. A team must separate patterns before it tells itself a proud story.
breakdown.fullRead:
Teams like to define products from the inside. They name capabilities, audiences, benefits, and brand attributes. Buyers write a different kind of record. They reveal what they trust by hiring the offering again when a familiar pressure returns. That record is the offering's resume.

The resume metaphor matters because it is earned. A person can claim a skill, but a resume is strongest when it shows repeated work under recognizable conditions. An offering works the same way. One strong story can point to a possible job. Many similar hires show what buyers have begun to rely on. The team should treat that reliance as strategic evidence.

This helps with focus. If a product is repeatedly hired to reduce anxiety before a high-stakes handoff, then a redesign that adds entertainment may distract from the earned job. If a service is repeatedly hired to make a novice feel capable in public, then expansion into expert features may ask buyers to trust something the service has not earned. The resume does not forbid growth. It asks whether growth extends an earned trust or demands a leap.

Basha, a school counselor at 2:27 p.m., may hear parents call the same hotline every grading cycle. The school may describe the hotline as information access. The repeated hire may be different: help me ask one specific question before I face my teenager tonight. If that is the resume, a giant resource portal could weaken the service by removing the human signal parents trust.

The caution is that repeated use can mislead when the team blends unlike jobs. A spreadsheet used every Friday by finance, every Tuesday by teachers, and every night by a caregiver may be one tool with three resumes. The team has to keep the circumstances attached. Otherwise it will claim broad trust where the market has granted only local trust.

Build the resume from repeated pressure, not from the loudest compliment. Write the job as a sentence with context attached: when this kind of buyer faces this kind of moment, they hire us for this kind of progress. Then test the next feature, message, or channel against that sentence. Does it strengthen the earned trust, or does it ask the market to believe a new claim?

The resume can grow, but growth has to be earned. A product may start by helping nervous beginners and later help confident users go farther. The bridge is proof. Without proof, expansion becomes wishful branding. With proof, the team can widen the promise without losing the job that made buyers come back.

The value of the resume is discipline. It disciplines messaging because the company should promise what buyers already rely on. It disciplines product work because changes should protect the job that earned the trust. It disciplines expansion because adjacent opportunities should be judged by whether the old resume helps or merely tempts the team. A market does not hand out identity all at once. It writes it through repeated hires.

examples.title: Ulric reads the muddy cards at the kayak counter

planSpec.requiredBeat: he sees the resume in repeated return cards

examples.scenario: Ulric clips another muddy return card to the nail at 5:32 p.m. behind the kayak counter, river grit drying on his forearm. Six cards this week mention nervous visitors, first paddle, and thank you for the calm launch. The brochure promises speed and coves. The cards tell a plainer record. Ulric needs to decide whether next season's offer is faster boats or the safest first hour on unfamiliar water.
examples.whatToDo: Read the repeated hires as a resume. Keep the nervous-guest circumstance attached, then design launch scripts, boat choice, and staffing around that earned trust.
examples.whyItMatters: The market is telling the shop what it relies on. Growth should extend that trust before it chases a more glamorous identity.

examples.title: Sonia names the inspection job in the boot shop

planSpec.requiredBeat: she hears what customers trust the shop to do repeatedly

examples.scenario: Sonia buffs black polish into a cracked boot at 4:40 p.m., the shop radio hissing under the sewing machine. "Same shine as March?" she asks. Harlan points to the inspection sticker on his clipboard. "Same sergeant, same hallway, same five seconds where he looks down first." Sonia smiles and stops reaching for the premium sole brochure. She has to choose whether to sell repair breadth or honor the job the customer has trusted twice already.
examples.whatToDo: Name the repeated inspection job. Record the hallway, the uniform standard, and the five-second glance as part of the shop's earned resume.
examples.whyItMatters: The customer is not asking for all possible leather skill. He is rehiring one reliable transformation before a recurring public judgment.

examples.title: Basha hesitates before calling the hotline a portal

planSpec.requiredBeat: she must decide how to describe repeated parent calls

examples.scenario: Basha stands at 2:27 p.m. beside the counselor office copier, call logs warm in her hand. Every grading cycle, parents ring the hotline for passwords they could find online. The principal wants to replace it with a resource portal. One note reads, "Needed one sentence before talking to Dena tonight." Basha's marker hovers over the planning board. She must decide whether the hotline's resume is information access or courage before a kitchen-table conversation.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the apparent task from the repeated hire. Study why parents call at grading time, what sentence they need, and what the human voice makes safer.
examples.whyItMatters: If the service has earned trust as pre-conversation support, replacing it with a portal may remove the very progress parents hire.

examples.title: Meryl predicts wedding cakes and finds rescue cakes

planSpec.stakes: repeat purchases reveal narrower trusted role
planSpec.requiredBeat: she sees reorders reveal the earned job

examples.scenario: Meryl sorts order slips at 6:14 a.m. beside the bakery mixer, predicting the custom wedding cakes prove the shop's prestige. The reorder stack says otherwise: office birthdays forgotten until 9:00, school celebrations with nut rules, sheet cakes picked up by embarrassed uncles. The reveal is humbling. The shop's strongest resume may be rescue without judgment. Meryl has to choose which promise goes on the window before Friday.
examples.whatToDo: Let the reorder pattern define the earned promise. Build ordering, pickup, and copy around fast rescue with dignity before advertising prestige.
examples.whyItMatters: Repeated hires show what buyers already trust. A prestige message could miss the job that keeps the register ringing every week.

examples.title: Keir sees the expansion outrun the product’s resume

planSpec.requiredBeat: he sees expansion asked for unearned trust

examples.scenario: Keir sits at 11:38 p.m. under the blue light of a release dashboard, refund emails open in a column. The team expanded from simple contractor checklists into full project finance. Existing customers loved the old app because it made Friday site walks impossible to forget. They did not trust it with payroll draws and lien notices. The postmortem is sharp: the product tried to put a new title on a resume the market had not written.
examples.whatToDo: Compare the expansion with the earned resume. Ask whether checklist trust gives permission to handle financial risk, and test that bridge before bundling.
examples.whyItMatters: Adjacent features are not automatically adjacent jobs. Buyers may trust an offering in one pressure zone and refuse it in another.

examples.title: Tanu rewrites reminders after three clinic rehires

planSpec.stakes: repeat use clarifies what reminder is hired for
planSpec.requiredBeat: she changes reminders after repeated hires reveal the role

examples.scenario: Tanu reviews appointment reminder replies at 7:07 a.m. in the clinic break room, oatmeal steaming beside the keyboard. Before, the message said your visit is tomorrow. After three months of replies asking whether childcare forms are still valid, she rewrites it: bring the yellow card, no new signature needed, stroller space is open. The reminder stops being a date ping and becomes proof the morning will not collapse.
examples.whatToDo: Let repeated replies rewrite the reminder's resume. Include the exact objects and assurances patients keep rehiring the message to confirm.
examples.whyItMatters: The reminder earned trust as a planning aid, not just a calendar alert. Protecting that job makes attendance easier for the patient.

questions.prompt: At 8:05 a.m., a bakery owner watches three regulars skip the croissants and buy plain coffee before the train doors close. The team is applying using repeated hires to identify what an offering has earned the right to be trusted for. Which next move best follows the jobs lens for this situation?
choices: Name the circumstance, the progress desired, and the substitutes already being used before changing features.
Rank customers by demographic similarity and average their requests into one roadmap item.
Ask the loudest buyer which feature would make the product seem more premium.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer starts with the pressured circumstance and the progress at stake. It treats observed behavior as evidence, then tests whether a real switch happens when that job is served better.

questions.prompt: During a 2:20 p.m. nurse handoff, a patient keeps using a pill organizer even after the app sends perfect reminders. The team is applying using repeated hires to identify what an offering has earned the right to be trusted for. Which interpretation should the team test before changing the product?
choices: Assume the buyer is irrational because the newer option has more features.
Treat the visible workaround as evidence of a struggling moment, then ask what it helps the buyer avoid or achieve.
Lower the price first, then look for explanations after volume changes.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer starts with the pressured circumstance and the progress at stake. It treats observed behavior as evidence, then tests whether a real switch happens when that job is served better.

questions.prompt: At 6:35 p.m., a teacher sees parents ignore the polished portal and text photos of homework to each other. The team is applying using repeated hires to identify what an offering has earned the right to be trusted for. Which question would reveal the progress being sought?
choices: Ask which color, size, and interface label each segment prefers.
Ask whether the buyer likes the brand more than competing brands.
Ask what changed right before the purchase, what felt hard about the old way, and what would count as progress now.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer starts with the pressured circumstance and the progress at stake. It treats observed behavior as evidence, then tests whether a real switch happens when that job is served better.

questions.prompt: On a rainy Saturday at 11:10 a.m., a hardware clerk notices renters buying tape, towels, and a cheap fan together. The team is applying using repeated hires to identify what an offering has earned the right to be trusted for. Which sign matters most for judging the real competitor?
choices: The substitute set the buyer compares in the moment, including awkward fixes outside the formal category.
The products displayed closest on the shelf, because they share the same category label.
The competitor with the highest advertising spend in the annual report.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer starts with the pressured circumstance and the progress at stake. It treats observed behavior as evidence, then tests whether a real switch happens when that job is served better.

questions.prompt: At 9:48 p.m., a founder reads cancellation notes that praise the product but mention setup dread in every third line. The team is applying using repeated hires to identify what an offering has earned the right to be trusted for. Which response avoids mistaking polite feedback for causal evidence?
choices: Treat every compliment as proof that the positioning is already clear.
Separate praise from switching evidence and look for anxiety, habit, push, and pull in the actual story.
Rewrite the website copy around the most flattering quote.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer starts with the pressured circumstance and the progress at stake. It treats observed behavior as evidence, then tests whether a real switch happens when that job is served better.

questions.prompt: Before a 7:30 a.m. board review, a transit planner compares riders who buy weekly passes with riders who pay one fare at a time. The team is applying using repeated hires to identify what an offering has earned the right to be trusted for. Which data cut would make the choice pattern less blurry?
choices: Blend all buyers into one persona so the team has a cleaner deck.
Focus only on lifetime value and ignore the purchase moment.
Split behavior by occasion and pressure, then compare what each group is trying to get done.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer starts with the pressured circumstance and the progress at stake. It treats observed behavior as evidence, then tests whether a real switch happens when that job is served better.

questions.prompt: At 4:12 p.m., a dentist sees a teenager use whitening strips carefully but abandon the prescribed night guard. The team is applying using repeated hires to identify what an offering has earned the right to be trusted for. Which design move respects the social and emotional pressure in the moment?
choices: Reduce the friction that makes the buyer feel exposed, guilty, rushed, or incompetent in that setting.
Add a technically superior feature even if it makes the buyer feel more watched.
Tell users they should care more about the functional benefit.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer starts with the pressured circumstance and the progress at stake. It treats observed behavior as evidence, then tests whether a real switch happens when that job is served better.

questions.prompt: While closing a library desk at 5:55 p.m., a clerk watches students book tiny rooms even when large tables are empty. The team is applying using repeated hires to identify what an offering has earned the right to be trusted for. Which observation most clearly points to a job rather than a category preference?
choices: The buyer says the category is interesting during a survey.
The buyer uses the option when a specific situation appears, even when other category choices are available.
The buyer recognizes the logo without remembering the purchase.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer starts with the pressured circumstance and the progress at stake. It treats observed behavior as evidence, then tests whether a real switch happens when that job is served better.

questions.prompt: At 10:03 a.m., a farm co-op manager hears growers ask for faster invoices while carrying handwritten notebooks. The team is applying using repeated hires to identify what an offering has earned the right to be trusted for. Which experiment would test whether the stated request matches the real hire?
choices: Ask the sales team to vote on the most elegant feature name.
Copy the category leader and wait for the market to notice.
Stage a small test around the moment of struggle and watch whether the buyer switches without being coached.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer starts with the pressured circumstance and the progress at stake. It treats observed behavior as evidence, then tests whether a real switch happens when that job is served better.

reviewCards.front: A customer praises the product but keeps using a clumsy workaround. What should you retrieve first?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the situation before the quote. Ask when the workaround appears, what progress it protects, and which anxiety keeps the customer from switching cleanly.

reviewCards.front: You see one product used in two different moments. What move keeps the analysis sharp?
reviewCards.back: Separate the moments. A shared product name can hide different jobs, different substitutes, and different standards for what good means.

reviewCards.front: A roadmap debate turns into feature ranking. How do you bring back the earned resume?
reviewCards.back: Put the buyer's struggling moment on the table, name the progress being hired, and judge each feature by whether it helps that movement happen.

reviewCards.front: A team has a beautiful story from one buyer. What question prevents overreach?
reviewCards.back: Ask which evidence repeats across similar circumstances and which details are local. A job story earns power through repeated hires, not through one vivid quote.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice reading demand from the situation before judging the product. The skill is to name the progress a person is trying to make, list the substitutes already in play, and test whether your offer helps that progress better than the current workaround.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a meeting starts ranking feature ideas, then write the buyer's exact moment of struggle at the top of the notes and force every option to answer how it improves the earned resume.
If you abandon a tool that looked sensible, then pause for one minute and name what the old habit protected before you replace it with another polished option.
If a repeated purchase feels oddly satisfying or oddly disappointing, then write the time, place, substitute, and desired progress before deciding what to buy next.
If someone asks for a surface fix, then ask what situation made the request urgent and what would feel better after the fix works.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, catch one choice while it is happening. Write the clock time, the place, the old workaround, the anxiety around switching, and one sentence naming the progress you are hiring the option to deliver.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, interview one person about a recent switch. Do not start with features. Reconstruct the moment, the push away from the old way, the pull of the new way, and the substitute they almost kept.

memorableLines.text: A resume is an earned record.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the metaphor into a retrieval line.

memorableLines.text: One story can inspire. A pattern earns trust.
A market does not hand out identity all at once.
memorableLines.why: It makes market identity feel earned over time.
